## Catalog description

**IMSE 456. Program and Project Management. 3 Credits.** Integrated approaches to managing
engineering, technology and business projects, addressing the project management lifecycle
including initiating, planning, executing, controlling and closing. Additional topics include
program management, portfolio management, and applying principles in a business environment.
Prereq or Coreq: Junior standing. Dual-listing: IMSE 656.

## How this course runs

Two sessions a week, and they do different jobs.

**Tuesday is concept.** The chapter's ideas, and usually a short case or discussion with a
decision in it. You leave knowing what is due.

**Thursday is studio, and it is hands-on and individual.** Every student works at their own machine
on the same three movements:

1. **Build — 25 minutes.** Work the concept out yourself first — by hand, in a spreadsheet, in a
   notebook, or with AI help. No professional software yet.
2. **Use — 20 minutes.** Do the same thing in the real tool: ProjectLibre, Smartsheet, Taiga or
   Power BI.
3. **Reconcile — 15 minutes.** Compare the two. If the numbers match, say so and say why you would
   trust them. **If they do not match exactly, explain how they differ and why** — a different
   definition, a different assumption, a rounding choice, or a mistake in one of them. Either
   answer is fine. Not looking is not.

**Then save and upload.** Save your own copy to your NDSU Google Drive or OneDrive, and upload the
file to Blackboard before you leave the room. The saved copy is yours to keep; the uploaded one is
what gets graded.

### How studios are graded

**Complete or incomplete.** A studio is complete when every item on its checklist is present in the
file you uploaded. That is the whole rubric — and you get written feedback on what you submitted.

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **Complete** | All checklist items present · reconciliation paragraph written · uploaded to Blackboard |
| **Incomplete** | Something on the checklist is missing |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Getting a different answer from the tool does not make a studio incomplete. Not explaining the
difference does.

## Course description

Project management as it is actually practised: the quantitative core — work breakdown, critical
path, PERT, resource levelling, crashing, earned value — alongside adaptive delivery and flow
metrics, with hybrid treated as the normal real-world case.

AI runs through every week. You will use it to draft project artifacts — work breakdowns, risk
registers, status reports, schedules — and then check what it produced against the real tool and
against your own work. In the final project your team builds a small AI-assisted project-management
workflow and writes about it publicly.

## Course objectives

By the end of the course you can:

1. Decide which delivery approach fits a given project and defend the choice against a specific alternative.
2. Build and interpret the core quantitative artifacts: WBS, CPM network, PERT distribution, resource-levelled schedule, crash analysis, EVM report.
3. Run the adaptive artifacts: product backlog, sprint mechanics, cumulative flow diagram, Little's Law.
4. Read the evidence critically — distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic.
5. Diagnose a failing project and propose interventions ranked by expected effect, not by convention.
6. Use AI to produce project artifacts, check them, and describe clearly where it helped and where it was wrong.

### Additional expectations for students enrolled in IMSE 656

Students enrolled under the graduate number complete the same components at a higher level of
expectation:

- **Studio assignments** require the reconciliation paragraph to cite the mechanism, not only the
  symptom — *which algorithm or formula choice produces this difference*, with a reference.
- **Final project** includes a short *methods justification*: why you chose the delivery approach,
  estimating method and control mechanism you did.
- **Final presentation** includes a five-minute defence against a challenge drawn from the
  counter-evidence for the position taken.

## Textbook and sequence

**Optional:** Larson &amp; Gray, *Project Management: The Managerial Process*, 2024 Release,
McGraw Hill. The course follows the book's chapter order with one displacement — the three
relationship chapters (10, 11, 12) move past 13 and 15, so that earned value arrives early enough
for your project to use it, and agile arrives after the predictive methods it trades against.

| Wk | Ch. | Subject | Wk | Ch. | Subject |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | 1 | Modern Project Management | 9 | 8 | Scheduling Resources and Costs |
| 2 | 2 | Strategy and Project Selection | 10 | 9 | Reducing Project Duration |
| 3 | 3 | Structure and Culture | 11 | 13 | Progress and Performance Measurement |
| 4 | 4 | Defining the Project | 12 | 15 | Agile Project Management |
| 5 | 5 | Estimating Times and Costs | 13 | 10 + 11 | Effective PM and Teams |
| 6 | 6 | Developing a Project Schedule | 14 | 12 | Outsourcing |
| 7 | 7 | Managing Risk | 15 | 14 + 16 | Closure and International |
| 8 | — | Review · **Midterm 15 Oct** | 16 | — | Final presentations |

: {tbl-colwidths="[5,8,37,5,8,37]"}

Everything you are assessed on is on this site. The book is a fuller treatment, not a requirement.
The authoritative week-by-week schedule with all due dates is on the [Schedule](schedule.qmd) page.

## If you work on lab computers only, this course still works
Almost everything runs in a browser. Where an install is a problem, the lab sheet gives you a
substitute — **Smartsheet** in place of ProjectLibre. Nothing is lost and nothing is graded
differently.

Software installation is never homework. Week 1's access form asks which machine you will work on
and which AI tools you can reach; your answer decides which version of every later lab sheet you
receive. It has no effect on your grade.

**Save nothing to a local disk.** Lab machines are wiped on reboot and laptops get left at home.
Set up a cloud folder in Week 1 and keep everything there.
:::

## Evaluation procedures and criteria

| Component | Weight | What it is |
|:--|--:|:--|
| Conceptual assignments | 25% | CA1–CA8, online multiple choice on terms, theory and the reasoning behind the methods. Auto-graded, lowest score dropped. |
| Studio assignments | 25% | SA1–SA14, **individual**, produced during Thursday studio and **uploaded to Blackboard before you leave** — graded with written feedback, no deadline to miss. Lowest two dropped. Five are graded against a full rubric — announced in advance — and the rest complete/incomplete against the published checklist. The reconciliation paragraph is read in every case. |
| Midterm examination | 20% | **Thursday 15 October, in class.** Closed book, closed notes, no computers or phones. Covers Chapters 1–7. |
| Final project | 30% | A semester-long project with an industry partner, in teams of four or five, including a published Medium article on the AI-assisted workflow your team built. FP1 5% · FP2 7% · FP3 8% · FP4 10%. See [Final Project](project.qmd). |

### Late work

**Late work is not accepted.** Deadlines are firm for the work that has one — conceptual
assignments and the final project deliverables.

**Studio assignments have no deadline.** They are produced in the Thursday session and uploaded to
Blackboard before you leave it, so the only way to miss one is to miss the session.

The dropped scores are your margin for a bad week: the lowest conceptual assignment and the two
lowest studio assignments are dropped automatically. If something serious happens, contact the
instructor **before** the deadline, or before the studio you will miss.

## Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

Generative AI use in this course is **permitted and expected, within the parameters below**. This
section is the course's AI policy under NDSU Policy 335: Code of Academic Responsibility and
Conduct. **Use outside these parameters is academic dishonesty** and is handled under that policy.

Much of this course is about using these tools well and knowing when they are wrong. That is a
learning objective, not a concession.

### Approved tools

**Gemini**, **Google Antigravity**, the **Gemini API** supplied through the course notebook, and
**Microsoft 365 Copilot** are approved for all permitted uses without further request. Any other
general-purpose assistant is approved on the same terms provided you name it in your disclosure.
Anything that is not a general-purpose assistant — a tool that completes assignments for you, or a
service you would have to send course material to — ask first.

Every student has access to Gemini and Antigravity, and **the instructor supplies API keys to
anyone who needs them**, so no graded work in this course depends on being able to buy a
subscription.

### How much AI, on which assessment

Each assessment carries a level from the Generative AI Acceptable Use Scale (Perkins et al., 2024).
The level is repeated on every lab sheet and assignment so you never have to guess.

| Assessment | Level | What that means here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Midterm examination** | **1 · Prohibited** | Closed book, closed notes, no computers or phones. The reasoning this tests is the reasoning you need when the tool is unavailable or wrong. |
| **Conceptual assignments (CA1–CA8)** | **1 · Prohibited during the attempt** | These are quizzes. Use AI freely to *study* — the Tutor prompts in [AI Studio](ai.qmd) are built for it — but not while the assessment is open. |
| **Studio assignments (SA1–SA14)** | **4 · Full use with documentation** | Generate freely, including the code. Every quantitative result arrives with the check that proves it, and the reconciliation paragraph must be your own reasoning. |
| **Final project (FP1–FP4)** | **5 · Full use with human oversight** | You are *required* to build and run an agent that maintains a live project artifact, and to report what it got wrong and how you caught it. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[26,20,54]"}

### How to disclose

Append this to any submission where AI was used. It takes two minutes and its absence is what turns
permitted use into a violation.

> **AI acknowledgement.** Tool used: [name]. What I used it for: [e.g. drafting the WBS].
> Prompt or transcript: [link or screenshot]. What I changed after reading its output: [edits].
> What it got wrong: [or "nothing I found"].

### The requirements, in short

- Acknowledge any significant AI contribution in submissions.
- Verify all AI-generated content for accuracy.
- Use AI ethically; violations constitute academic dishonesty.
- **AI is forbidden for quizzes and tests** — the midterm and the conceptual assignments.

### Data, confidentiality and privacy

This matters more here than in most courses, because your final project involves a real
organization's information.

- **Do not put a partner organization's confidential information into any AI tool.** Costs,
  contracts, customer data, unreleased plans, anything they asked you to protect. Generalize the
  problem or use synthetic numbers instead. If you are unsure whether something is confidential,
  it is.
- **Do not put anyone's personal information into an AI tool** — classmates', a partner's staff,
  your own beyond what you would post publicly.
- **Do not upload another student's work.** Their submissions are their educational records.
- If a partner asks for a written commitment about AI use, bring it to the instructor before you
  agree to anything. Do not sign on behalf of NDSU.

## Instructor use of AI — disclosure

You are being asked to label, verify and own your AI use. The same standard applies to the person
teaching you, so here is exactly how AI was used to build this course.

**What AI did.** Working from my own outlines, notes and the textbook's chapter structure, I used
generative AI to help organize the course: to sequence the sixteen weeks against Larson's chapters
and argue about where the displacement should fall; to draft and edit lecture notes, the mini-cases
you read on Tuesdays, and the studio lab sheets you work from on Thursdays; to generate the studio
datasets and compute every answer key programmatically; to draft rubrics and the "done looks like"
checklists; and to build this website.

**What AI did not do, and will not do.**

- **It does not grade you.** No AI system assigns or recommends a mark in this course.
- **Your work is not uploaded to any third-party AI system**, for grading or for any other purpose.
  Your submissions are educational records under FERPA and they stay in Blackboard.
- **It does not decide anything.** Every sequencing choice, assessment weight, rubric criterion and
  final grade is mine.

**What I verify.** Every factual claim, empirical figure and citation in these materials is checked
against a primary source before it is published — the sources are listed in
[AI Studio](ai.qmd#the-source-shelf) so you can check them too. Every numerical answer key is
computed in code rather than by hand, precisely because a hand-worked key is where errors hide and
an error in a key is worse than an error in a lecture.

**Where you can see it.** This site is public and so is
[the repository that builds it](https://github.com/harunpirim/IMSE456). If you want to see how a
course is actually assembled, including the parts a model drafted, you can read the source. That
transparency is the point: I am asking you to show your work, so I show mine.

**If AI use in this course changes** — a new tool, a new use — it will be announced on Blackboard
and this section updated. If you think something here was AI-generated and is wrong, tell me. You
will be right often enough to make it worth asking, and finding it is exactly the skill this course
is trying to build.
